title: remobi.app: Don't change your terminal workflow for mobile

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

summary: Connor Adams introduces Remoby, an open-source progressive web app designed to let developers check on and control terminal-based AI coding agents from their mobile phones without altering their existing terminal workflows. The presentation begins with the common problem: developers feel compelled to check on their agents while away from their computers, but existing solutions have significant limitations. Happy only works with Claude Code and uses an untrusted relay server. Claude's built-in mobile handoff requires manual activation and limits you to one tool. Generic terminal apps on phones suffer from cumbersome SSH key management, awkward touch controls, and poor integration with workflows like tmux. Adams demonstrates tmux, a terminal multiplexer that functions as a window manager for terminals, supporting multiple panes, windows, custom key bindings, and status displays. He shows running multiple coding agents simultaneously, using lazygit and critique for code review, and managing system resources. His tmux setup was largely vibe-coded with AI assistance. The core of Remoby is that it exposes tmux sessions to a mobile interface. As a progressive web app, it works on iOS and Android, running a server on the developer's machine. Users can scroll through panes, zoom in on individual panes by double-clicking, switch agents to plan mode, and access tools like lazygit. The interface supports touch gestures and includes custom key bindings translated for touch-screen use. For connectivity, Remoby defaults to Tailscale for secure tunneling, though Cloudflare tunnels or ngrok are also supported. Adams explicitly warns that exposing the server directly to the public internet would compromise the machine. Setup is facilitated through an installable skill that helps configure tmux and creates touch-friendly key bindings. The tool is open source, available on GitHub, and installable via NPM. During Q&A, Adams clarified that Remoby simply calls tmux and logs into the session, and that security depends on the tunneling solution chosen.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Connor Adams introduces himself and Remoby. He asks the audience about checking AI agents on phones and describes the compulsion to monitor agents while away from the desk, motivating the need for a mobile solution.

sections.title: Existing Alternatives and Limitations
sections.summary: Reviews existing options: Happy (Claude Code only, untrusted relay server), Claude's built-in handoff (manual, limits to one tool), and terminal apps on phones (SSH key management, touch controls, workflow integration issues). Introduces tmux as his preferred portable setup.

sections.title: tmux Demonstration
sections.summary: Demonstrates tmux as a window manager for terminals with multiple panes, windows, custom key bindings, and status displays. Shows running multiple agents, using lazygit and critique for code review, killing processes on occupied ports, and customizing workflows. Notes the setup was vibe-coded with AI.

sections.title: Remoby Mobile App Demonstration
sections.summary: Shows Remoby as a progressive web app on a phone connected to the same tmux session. Demonstrates scrolling through panes, double-click to zoom, switching to plan mode, accessing lazygit and critique tools with touch gestures. Acknowledges the UI is minimal but functional.

sections.title: Setup, Conclusion, and Q&A
sections.summary: Explains setup via an installable skill that configures tmux and creates touch-screen key bindings. Mentions open-source availability on GitHub and NPM. Q&A covers: Remoby calls tmux directly and logs into sessions, connectivity uses Tailscale by default (also Cloudflare tunnels, ngrok), and exposing the server publicly would compromise the machine.

demonstrations: Demonstrated tmux with multiple panes running different coding agents simultaneously
Showed lazygit for reviewing git diffs within tmux
